nameStory: The name 'thorow-wax' comes from this plant's most distinctive feature - its unusual leaves that appear to be pierced right through by the stem, as if someone took a awl and poked it 'thorow' (through) a waxy leaf. This strange leaf arrangement made early botanists think the stem was growing directly through the leaf blade, creating the memorable common name that's stuck for centuries.
description: Thorow-wax is an unusual annual herb in the carrot family that grows 1-3 feet tall with a distinctive upright, branching habit. What makes this plant immediately recognizable are its blue-green, oval leaves that appear to be completely pierced by the stem - the stem seems to grow right through the middle of each leaf. The small yellowish-green flowers are clustered in umbrella-like groups typical of the carrot family. Originally from Europe and North Africa, it's now established as a weed in disturbed areas across the eastern United States.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval, blue-green leaves that appear pierced by the stem - the stem literally passes through the center of each leaf blade, creating a distinctive 'cup and saucer' effect that you can feel with your finger

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny yellowish-green flowers arranged in small, flat-topped umbrella clusters (umbels) typical of the carrot family, each cluster only 1-2 inches across with 5-10 rays

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Erect annual herb growing 1-3 feet tall with a smooth, often waxy-feeling stem that branches in the upper portion, giving it a candelabra-like appearance

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Leaves feel smooth and somewhat waxy to the touch, with a distinctive blue-green or gray-green color that stands out among other weedy plants

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, oval, ribbed seeds typical of the carrot family, about 1/8 inch long, turning brown when mature and often persisting on the dried umbels

habitat: Look for thorow-wax in disturbed soils, particularly cultivated fields, gardens, roadsides, and waste areas with rich, well-drained soil. It thrives in areas with regular soil disturbance and full sun exposure. In New England, it's most commonly found as an agricultural weed in crop fields and along field edges.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as small rosettes with the distinctive perfoliate leaves already visible, making identification possible even in the seedling stage.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period when the yellowish-green umbrella clusters are most prominent, and the blue-green perfoliate leaves are at their most distinctive.
seasonality.fall: Plants begin to turn yellow and brown, but the dried stems with seed heads often persist, and the perfoliate leaf arrangement remains visible on dried specimens.
seasonality.winter: Dead stems with old seed heads may persist through early winter, but plants are annual so no living parts remain above ground.

funFact: Thorow-wax is one of the few plants in North America where the stem actually grows completely through the leaf blade - if you hold a leaf up to the light, you can see the stem passing right through the middle like nature's own magic trick, earning it the botanical term 'perfoliate' meaning 'through the leaf.'
confusionNotes: The perfoliate leaves make thorow-wax almost impossible to confuse with any other plant in New England - no other species has leaves that are so obviously pierced by the stem. The closest might be some Eupatorium species, but they have opposite leaves and very different flowers.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being in the carrot family (Apiaceae), thorow-wax looks nothing like the typical carrot-family plants most people know - its flowers are much smaller and less showy than Queen Anne's lace, and its leaves are completely different from the finely divided foliage typical of most family members.
compareHints: Thorow-wax is the only Bupleurum species commonly found in New England. Compared to other carrot family members like Queen Anne's lace or wild parsnip, it's much smaller and less conspicuous, with tiny flower clusters rather than large, showy umbels. The perfoliate leaves immediately distinguish it from all other regional carrot family species, which typically have finely divided, feathery foliage.
